In the nucleus of the host, the newly transcribed DNA incorporates into the host DNA and is transcribed into RNA when the host cell undergoes normal transcription.

Reverse transcriptase.Definition: Enzyme carried by retroviruses that function to convert RNA to DNA.

Rf.Definition: Variable that indicates the relative rate at which one molecule migrates compared to the solvent of a paper chromatograph.

Ribosomes.Definition: Host organelle for protein synthesis composed of a large subunit and a small subunit. Ribosomes are built in the nucleolus.

RNA polymerase.Definition: Enzyme that runs transcription and adds the appropriate nucleotides to the 3′ end of the growing strand.

RNA splicing.Definition: Process that removes introns from newly produced mRNA and then glues exons back together to produce the final product.

Root.Definition: Portion of the plant that is below the ground.

Root cap.Definition: Protective structure found around the apical meristem of a root that keeps it together as it pushes through the soil.

Root hairs.Definition: Hairs extending off the surface of root tips that increase the surface area for absorption of water and nutrients from the soil.

Root pressure.Definition: Driving force that contributes to the movement of water through the xylem of a plant.

Rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER).Definition: Membrane-bound organelle with ribosomes on the cytoplasmic surface of the cell. Proteins produced by RER are often secreted and carried by vesicles to the Golgi apparatus for further modification.

rRNA.Definition: Ribosomal RNA, which makes up a huge portion of ribosomes.

Rubisco.Definition: Enzyme that catalyzes the first step of the Calvin cycle in C3 plants.

S phase.Definition: The DNA is copied so that each daughter cell has a complete set of chromosomes at the conclusion of the cell cycle.

Saprobe.Definition: Organism that feeds off dead organisms.

Saturated fat.Definition: Fat that contains no double bonds. It is associated with heart disease and atherosclerosis.

Savanna.Definition: Grassland that contains a spattering of trees found all over South America, Australia, and Africa. Savanna soil tends to be low in nutrients, while temperatures tend to run high.

Sclerenchyma cells.Definition: Plant cells that function as protection and mechanical support.

Search image.Definition: Mental image that assists animals during foraging. It directs them to food of interest.

Second messenger.Definition: Molecule that serves as an intermediary, activating other proteins and enzymes in a chemical reaction.

Secondary consumers.Definition: Consumers that obtain energy through consumption of the primary consumers.

Secondary immune response.Definition: Memory cells are the basis for this efficient response to invaders.

Secondary oocyte.Definition: An oocyte that has half the genetic information of the parent cell, but the majority of its cytoplasm.

Secondary plant growth.Definition: Growth that leads to an increase in plant girth.

Secondary sex characteristics.Definition: The noticeable physical characteristics that differ between males and females such as facial hair, deepness of voice, breasts, and muscle distribution.

Secondary spermatocyte.Definition: Cells formed during spermatogenesis that give rise to spermatids and even- tually sperm.

Secondary structure.Definition: The three-dimensional arrangement of a protein caused by hydrogen bonding.

Secondary succession.Definition: Succession in an area that previously had stable plant and/or animal life but has since been disturbed by some major force such as a forest fire.

Semiconservative DNA replication.Definition: Before the parent strand is copied, the DNA unzips, with each single strand serving as a template for the creation of a new double strand. One strand of DNA from the parent goes to one daughter cell; the second parent strand goes to the second daughter cell.

Seminal vesicles.Definition: Structures that dump fluids into the ejaculatory duct to send along with the sperm, providing three important advantages to the sperm: energy by adding fructose; power to progress through the female reproductive system by adding prostaglandin (which stimulates uterine contraction); and mucus, which helps the sperm swim more effectively.

Sensory neurons.Definition: Nerve cells that receive and communicate information from the sensory environment.

Septae.Definition: Structures that divide the hypha filaments of fungi into different compartments.

Sex pili.Definition: Bacterial appendage vital to process of conjugation.

Sex ratio.Definition: Proportion of males and females in a given population.

Sexual selection.Definition: The process by which certain characters are selected for because they aid in mate acquisition.

Shoots.Definition: Parts of a plant that are above the ground.

Short-day plants.Definition: Plants, such as poinsettias, that flower if exposed to nighttime conditions longer than a critical period of length.

Sickle cell anemia.Definition: A recessive disease caused by the substitution of a single amino acid in the hemoglobin protein of red blood cells, leaving hemoglobin less able to carry oxygen and also causing the hemoglobin to deform to a sickle shape when the oxygen content of the blood is low. The sickling causes pain, muscle weakness, and fatigue.

Sieve-tube elements.Definition: Functionally mature cells of the phloem that are alive.

Sink.Definition: Site of carbohydrate consumption in plants.

Skeletal muscle.Definition: Striated muscle that controls voluntary activities and contains multiple nuclei.

Smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER).Definition: Membrane-bound organelle involved in lipid synthesis, detoxification, and carbohydrate metabolism; has no ribosomes on its cytoplasmic surface.

Smooth muscle.Definition: Involuntary muscle that contracts slowly and is controlled by the autonomic nervous system (ANS).

Sodium-potassium pump.Definition: A mechanism that actively moves potassium into the cell and sodium out of the cell against their respective concentration gradients to maintain appropriate levels inside the cell.

Solute.Definition: A substance dissolved in a solution.

Somatotropic hormone (STH).Definition: A hormone that stimulates protein synthesis and growth in the body.

Somite.Definition: Structure that gives rise to the muscles and vertebrae in mammals.

Source.Definition: Site of carbohydrate creation in plants.

Southern blotting.Definition: Procedure used to determine if a particular sequence of nucleotides is present in a sample of DNA.

Specialized transduction.Definition: Transduction involving a virus in the lysogenic cycle that shifts to the lytic cycle. If it accidentally brings with it a piece of the host DNA as it pulls out of the host chromosome, this DNA could find its way into another cell.

Speciation.Definition: The process by which new species evolve.

Species.Definition: A group of interbreeding (or potentially interbreeding) organisms.

Specific immunity.Definition: Complicated multilayered defense mechanism that protects a host against foreign invasion.

Spectrophotometer.Definition: Machine used to determine how much light can pass through a sample.

Spermatids.Definition: Immature sperm that enter the epididymis, where their waiting game begins and maturation is completed.

Spermatogenesis.Definition: Process by which the male gametes are formed. Four haploid sperm are produced during each meiotic cycle. This does not begin until puberty, and it occurs in the seminiferous tubules.

Spongy mesophyll.Definition: Region of a plant where the cells are more loosely arranged, aiding in the passage of CO2 to cells performing photosynthesis.

Sporophyte.Definition: The diploid multicellular stage of the plant life cycle.

Sporozoite.Definition: Small infectious form that apicomplexa protists take to spread from place to place.

Stabilizing selection.Definition: This describes selection for the mean of a population for a given allele; has the effect of reducing variation in a given population.

Stamen.Definition: Male structure of a flower that contains the pollen-producing anther.

Starch.Definition: Storage polysaccharide made of glucose molecules; seen in plants.

Start codon (AUG).Definition: Codon that establishes the reading frame for protein formation.

Stem cells.Definition: Cells that give rise to the immune cells of the human body.

Steroid hormones.Definition: Lipid-soluble molecules that pass through the cell membrane and combine with cytoplasmic proteins. These complexes pass through to the nucleus to interact with chromosomal proteins and directly affect transcription in the nucleus.

Steroids.Definition: Lipids composed of four carbon rings. Examples include cholesterol, estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone.

Sticky ends.Definition: Single-stranded DNA fragments formed when DNA is treated with restriction enzymes. These fragments find and reconnect with other fragments with the same ends.

Stigma.Definition: Flower structure that functions as the receiver of pollen.

Stomata.Definition: Structure through which CO2 enters a plant, and water vapor and O2 leave.

Stop codons (UGA, UAA, UAG).Definition: Codons that stop the production of a protein.

Storage diseases.Definition: Diseases such as Tay-Sachs that are caused by the absence of a particular lysosomal hydrolytic enzyme.

Strain.Definition: Groups into which bacterial species are placed.

Stroma.Definition: The inner fluid portion of the chloroplast that plays host to the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis.

Style.Definition: Pathway in a flower that leads to the ovary.

Succession.Definition: Shift in the local composition of species in response to changes that occur over time.

Sulfhydryl group.Definition: A functional group that helps stabilize the structure of many proteins.

Survivorship curves.Definition: A tool used to study the population dynamics of species.

Symbiosis.Definition: A relationship between two different species that can be classified as one of three main types: commensalism, mutualism, and parasitism.

Sympathetic nervous system.Definition: Branch of the autonomic nervous system that gets the body ready to move.

Sympatric speciation.Definition: Interbreeding ceases even though no physical barrier prevents it. Can occur as a result of polyploidy and balanced polymorphism.

Symplast pathway.Definition: Movement of water and nutrients through the living portion of plant cells.

Synaptic knob.Definition: The end of the axon. This is where calcium gates are opened in response to the changing potential, which causes vesicles to release substances called neurotransmitters (NTs) into the synaptic gap between the axon and the target cell. These NTs diffuse across the gap, causing a new impulse in the target cell.

Tactile communication.Definition: Communication that involves the use of touch in the conveying of a message.

Taiga.Definition: Biome characterized by lengthy, cold, and wet winters. This biome is found in Canada and has gymnosperms as its prominent plant life. This biome contains coniferous forests (pine and other needle-bearing trees).

Tapeworm.Definition: Parasitic flatworm whose adult form lives in vertebrates.

Taproot system.Definition: System of roots found in many dicots that starts as one thick root and divides into many smaller lateral roots, which serve as an anchor for the plant.

TATA box.Definition: Group of nucleotides found in the promoter region that assists in binding of RNA polymerase to the DNA strand for transcription.

Taxis.Definition: The reflex movement toward or away from a stimulus.

Taxonomy.Definition: The field of biology that classifies organisms according to the presence or absence of shared characteristics in an effort to discover evolutionary relationships between species.

Tay-Sachs disease.Definition: A fatal genetic storage disease that renders the body unable to break down a particular type of lipid.

Temperate deciduous forest.Definition: A biome that is found in regions that experience cold winters where plant life is dormant, alternating with warm summers that provide enough moisture to keep large trees alive.

Temperate grasslands.Definition: Found in regions with cold winter temperatures. The soil of this biome is considered to be among the most fertile of all.

Termination site.Definition: Region of DNA that tells the polymerase when transcription should conclude.

Territoriality.Definition: Scenario in which territorial individuals defend their territory against other individuals.

Tertiary structure.Definition: The 3D (three-dimensional) arrangement of a protein caused by interaction among the various R groups of the amino acids involved.

Test cross.Definition: Crossing of an organism of unknown dominant genotype with an organism that is homozygous recessive for the trait, resulting in offspring with observable phenotypes. Test crosses are used to determine the unknown genotype.

Testis.Definition: The site of sperm and testosterone production in animals; males have two testes, located in the scrotum.

Testosterone.Definition: Sex hormone produced in testes that stimulates the growth of male sex characteristics.

Thermoacidophiles.Definition: Archaebacteria that live in hot, acidic environments.

Thermoregulation.Definition: The process by which temperature is maintained.

Thigmotropism.Definition: A plant's growth in response to touch.

Thylakoid membrane system.Definition: Inner membrane that winds through the stroma of a chloroplast. Site of the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.

Thymine dimers.Definition: Thymine nucleotides located adjacent to one another on the DNA strand bind together when excess exposure to UV light occurs. This can negatively affect replication of DNA and assist in the creation of further mutations.

Thymosin.Definition: Hormone involved in the development of the T cells of the immune system.

Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).Definition: A hormone that stimulates the synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones, which regulate the rate of metabolism in the body.

Thyroxin.Definition: Hormone released by the thyroid gland that functions in the control of metabolic activities in the body.

Tongue.Definition: Structure that functions to move food around while we chew and helps to arrange the food into a swallowable bolus.

Trachea.Definition: The tunnel that leads air into the thoracic cavity.

Tracheid cells.Definition: Xylem cells in charge of water transport in gymnosperm.

Transcription factors.Definition: Helper proteins that assist RNA polymerase in finding and attaching to the promoter region.

Transduction.Definition: The movement of genes from one cell to another by phages.

Transformation.Definition: The transfer of genetic material from one cell to another, resulting in a genetic change in the receiving cell.

Translocation.Definition: Movement of the ribosome along the mRNA in such a way that the A site becomes the P site and the next tRNA comes into the new A site carrying the next amino acid.

Translocation (plants).Definition: Movement of carbohydrates through the phloem.

Transpiration.Definition: Process by which plants lose water by evaporation through their leaves.

Trichinosis.Definition: Disease found in humans caused by a roundworm that infects meat products.

Trophic levels.Definition: Hierarchy of energy levels that describe the energy distribution of a planet.

Trophoblast.Definition: Forms the placenta for the developing fetus, and aids in attachment to the endometrium. This structure also produces human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which maintains the endometrium by ensuring the continued production of progesterone.

Tropical forests.Definition: These forests consist primarily of tall trees that form a thick cover, which blocks the light from reaching the floor of the forest (where there is little growth). Tropical rainforests are known for their rapid recycling of nutrients and contain the greatest diversity of species.

Tropism.Definition: Plant growth that occurs in response to an environmental stimulus such as sunlight or gravity.

Tropomyosin.Definition: Regulatory protein known to block the actin-myosin binding site and prevent muscular contraction in the absence of calcium.

Trypsin.Definition: Enzyme that cuts protein bonds in the small intestine.

Tundra.Definition: This biome experiences extremely cold winters during which the ground freezes completely. Short shrubs or grasses that are able to withstand the difficult conditions dominate.

Turner syndrome.Definition: Affects females who are missing an X chromosome.

Umbilical cord.Definition: Structure that transports oxygen, food, and waste (CO2) between the embryo and the placenta.

Uniform distribution.Definition: Scenario in which individuals are evenly spaced out across a given geographic area.

Unsaturated fat.Definition: Fat that contains one or more double bonds; found in plants.

Uracil.Definition: The nucleotide that replaces thymine in RNA.

Urethra.Definition: Exit point for both urine and sperm from males and urine for females.

Uterus.Definition: Site of embryo attachment and development in mammals.

Vaccination.Definition: Inoculation of medicine into a patient in an effort to prime the immune system to be prepared to fight a specific sickness if confronted in the future.

Vacuole.Definition: A storage organelle that is large in plant cells but small in animal cells.

Vas deferens.Definition: Tunnel that connects the epididymis to the urethra.

Vascular cambium.Definition: A cylinder of tissue that extends the length of the stem and root and gives rise to the secondary xylem and phloem.

Vascular cylinder.Definition: Structure in plants that is composed of cells that produce the lateral roots of the plant.

Vector.Definition: Agent that moves DNA from one source to another.

Veins.Definition: Structures that return blood to the heart.

Vena cava system.Definition: System of veins that returns deoxygenated blood from the body to the heart to be reoxygenated in the lungs.

Vessel elements.Definition: Xylem cells in charge of water transport in angiosperms. More efficient than tracheid cells.

Vestigial characters.Definition: Characters that are no longer useful, although they once were.

Viral envelope.Definition: Protective barrier that surrounds some viruses but also helps them attach to cells.

Viroids.Definition: Plant viruses that are only a few hundred nucleotides in length.

Virus.Definition: A parasitic infectious agent that is unable to survive outside a host organism. Viruses do not contain enzymes for metabolism or ribosomes for protein synthesis.

Visual communication.Definition: Communication through the use of the visual senses.

Water biomes.Definition: Both freshwater and marine biomes, which occupy the majority of the surface of the Earth.

Water cycle.Definition: The Earth is covered in water. A lot of this water evaporates each day and returns to the clouds. This water is then returned to the earth in the form of precipitation.

Water potential.Definition: The force that drives water to move in a given direction. Combination of solute potential and pressure potential.

Water vascular system.Definition: Series of tubes and canals within echinoderms that play a role in ingestion of food, movement, and gas exchange.

Wild-type phenotype.Definition: The normal phenotype for a characteristic in fruit flies and other organisms.

Within-sex competition.Definition: Competition for mates between members of the same sex.

Wobble.Definition: Nucleotides in the third position of an anticodon are able to pair with many nucleotides instead of just their normal partner.

X-inactivation.Definition: During the development of the female embryo, one of the two X chromosomes in each cell remains coiled as a Barr body whose genes are not expressed. A cell expresses the alleles of the active X chromosome only.

Xylem.Definition: The “superhighway,” or important part of the vascular tissue in plants, through which water and nutrients travel throughout the plant. Also functions as a support structure that strengthens the plant.

Yolk sac.Definition: Derived from the hypoblast, this is the site of early blood cell formation in humans and the source of nutrients for bird and reptile embryos.

Zone of cell division.Definition: Region at the tip of a root formed by the actively dividing cells of the apical meristem.

Zone of elongation.Definition: Cells of this region elongate tremendously during plant growth.

Zone of maturation.Definition: Region in the plant where cells differentiate into their final forms.
